name: yesno_v0
data_seen: none. No BioASQ item, no feature statistics, no accuracy feedback.
basis: BioASQ overview papers (Tsatsaronis et al. 2015, Nentidis et al. 2020 to 2025), BioASQ-QA data paper (Krithara et al. 2023), and the general literature on artefacts in crowd- and expert-written yes/no questions (Gururangan et al. 2018, Poliak et al. 2018, Clark et al. 2019 BoolQ). Where a weight rests on a hypothesis about how experts construct 'no' questions rather than on a published finding, it is marked hypothesis.
decision: score = sum(weight * feature); predict yes if score > 0 else no

justification.bias: Published finding. BioASQ yes/no sets have been reported as skewed towards yes in the training data and in several test batches (overview papers from BioASQ 6 onwards discuss the imbalance and the move to macro F1 for that reason). The prior is set so that a question with no other cue is answered yes.
justification.neg: Published finding for NLI (Gururangan et al. 2018): negation words are the strongest cue for the negative class. Hypothesis for BioASQ: experts turning a true statement into a question rarely insert negation, so a negated question is more often constructed to be false.
justification.universal: Hypothesis. Universal and exclusive claims (only, all, always, exclusively) are the standard way to make a true biomedical statement false, since most biomedical regularities have exceptions. Also the classic false-answer pattern in BoolQ-style sets.
justification.possibility: Hypothesis. Possibility claims (can X cause Y, is it possible that) are weak and therefore usually true in the literature the question was written from.
justification.association: Hypothesis. Association, involvement and regulation claims are written from a paper reporting that association, so the default answer is yes.
justification.identity: Hypothesis. Questions asking whether two named things are the same, identical or interchangeable are typically written to test a known distinction, so the answer is usually no.
justification.comparison: Hypothesis, weak. Comparative questions are often constructed by flipping the direction of a known difference.
justification.has_number: Hypothesis. A specific number in a yes/no question (chromosome number, count of members, percentage) is a common point of alteration when writing a false question. Krithara et al. 2023 describe experts producing questions with definite answers, and altering a detail is the natural way to get a definite no.
justification.approval: Hypothesis. Questions about regulatory approval of a named drug are mostly written about drugs that are approved.
justification.contradiction: Hypothesis. Words signalling dispute or disproof mark questions written to be answered no.
justification.efficacy: Set near zero. Efficacy questions go both ways: trial-based questions are often constructed from negative trials.
justification.prevent: Hypothesis, weak. Strong claims of prevention or cure are frequently false in the biomedical literature.
justification.len_gt_15: Set near zero. No published finding on length for BioASQ yes/no. Kept so the regenerated weights can disagree with it.
justification.starts_is_are: Near zero. Question form alone is not expected to carry much.
justification.starts_can: Small positive, same reasoning as possibility.
justification.two_entities: Hypothesis, weak. Two named entities in the question suggest an association question written from a paper reporting it.
